opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a distinction I think about a lot, because those two moments meant very different things for us at DeepMind.

AlphaGo was the moment where we showed something was *possible*. We took a huge corpus of human expert games, trained a policy network to imitate people, and then layered reinforcement learning and search on top. The system ended up superhuman, but its starting point was human knowledge. It stood on our shoulders. To me that's roughly where large language models are today. We pre-train on essentially the whole internet, which is the human data. Then we do post-training, RLHF, and more recently reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks to push past pure imitation. And we're starting to see glimpses of the move 37 kind of thing, where a model finds a solution or a line of reasoning that a person wouldn't naturally have come up with.

AlphaZero was a different kind of statement. We threw away the human data entirely. The system learned from the rules of the game alone, through self-play, and it got *stronger* than the version bootstrapped from humans. That was the surprising part. Human data wasn't just unnecessary; in some sense it was a ceiling, a bias we had to unlearn. And the same algorithm worked across Go, chess, and shogi with essentially no changes. So it was generality plus independence from human priors.

So for language models, an AlphaZero moment would mean a system that improves mainly through its own experience. It would generate its own problems, attempt them, check itself against some grounded signal, and keep getting better without being bottlenecked by how much human-written text exists. The hard part, and the reason we're not there yet, is the reward. In Go, you know who won. The environment gives you perfect, cheap feedback. In the open-ended real world, you don't have a clean win/loss signal for most things. Math and code are the closest analogues because you can verify answers, which is exactly why that's where we're seeing the fastest progress with RL.

So my short version: the AlphaGo moment is "superhuman performance built on top of human knowledge," and I think we're living through that now in narrow domains. The AlphaZero moment is "superhuman performance that comes from the system's own experience, with human data as optional at best." That one depends on solving verification and reward in much broader domains. I think it's coming, but it's a qualitatively different step, not just more scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Ioannis: Yeah, I think it's a useful distinction, and it comes straight out of what happened with Go. With AlphaGo, the system started from human data. We had something like thirty million positions from strong amateur games, and we trained a policy network to imitate those moves. Then we did reinforcement learning on top of that, with self-play, and that's what pushed it past the human level. So the human data was the foundation, and RL was the thing that took it further. The AlphaGo moment is when you take all the accumulated human knowledge, you bootstrap from it, and then you use search and reinforcement learning to go beyond it.

AlphaZero was different in kind, not just in degree. We threw away the human data entirely. The only thing the system had was the rules of the game, and a reward signal at the end: did you win or did you lose. Everything else was discovered through self-play. And what was striking wasn't just that it got stronger, it was that it played differently. It wasn't constrained by human priors about what good Go looks like. Some of the opening patterns that people had played for hundreds of years, it just discarded, and it found others.

So when I map that onto language models, I'd say we are clearly in the AlphaGo phase right now. The models are pretrained on essentially all human text, which is the imitation step. And then we do RL on top, sometimes with human preferences, more recently with verifiable rewards in domains like mathematics and code, where you can actually check if the answer is correct. That's genuinely producing capabilities beyond what's in the training data, in the sense that the models can solve problems no one wrote the solution to. That's the AlphaGo moment for LLMs, and I think we've already had it, or are in the middle of it.

The AlphaZero moment would be something else. It would be a system that learns to reason, or to use language, or to do science, without needing the human corpus as a starting point. And honestly, I'm not sure that's the right goal for language. Go has a perfect simulator and a perfectly defined reward. Language doesn't. The reward for most of what we care about is defined by humans, and the environment is the world, which we can't simulate perfectly. So the question isn't really "can we get rid of human data," it's "in which domains can we build a reward signal good enough that self-improvement takes off." Math is close. Code is close. Formal verification, maybe. Those are the places where I'd look for an AlphaZero moment first, because they're the places where you can actually tell the model, unambiguously, that it was right or wrong. And once you have that, the loop can run by itself.

r002.rationale: It describes the AlphaZero moment as something that would be different and identifies domains where it might happen first, indicating it has not happened yet.

r003.rationale: It describes learning without a human corpus and a self-running loop with reliable rewards, but does not define the moment as more compute directly increasing intelligence without human intervention.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is where the learning signal comes from. AlphaGo learned from human games first, and then improved through self-play. AlphaZero skipped the human examples and learned through self-play, using the rules of the game and whether it won or lost.

For language models, an AlphaGo moment would be taking a model pretrained on human text and using reinforcement learning to push it beyond what it can do by imitating that text. An AlphaZero moment would be a system that can generate its own experience and learn from it, with much less dependence on human examples.

The difficult part is that language doesn’t have a single, clear winning condition. In Go, you know who won. For a general-purpose model, you need a way to judge whether what it did was actually better. So I think the key is whether the system can keep improving through its own experience, with a reliable signal that grounds that improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is where the learning signal comes from. AlphaGo started by learning from human games and then improved through reinforcement learning. AlphaZero removed that initial dependence on human games: given the rules, it learned through self-play.

For language models, an AlphaGo moment would be a system that starts from human knowledge, as today’s models do through pretraining, and then uses reinforcement learning to go substantially beyond what people have demonstrated. An AlphaZero moment would be a system that can generate its own learning experience and keep improving without relying on new human examples.

The difficult part is defining what makes an answer better. In Go, you know who won. With language, you need a reliable learning signal across a much wider range of tasks. So the question is whether we can build environments where models can explore, get meaningful feedback, and discover things we didn’t already know.
